Thanks Sam — the sample is helpful. A few technical notes we can cover in the deep-dive so the migration is smooth: 

1) Vector dimensions & cost tradeoffs:
- Keeping 1536-d preserves current quality; downsizing to 1024/768 can cut storage and network cost ~25-40% depending on quantization. We'll run an A/B on recall for a representative query set.

2) Normalization best-practices:
- If you currently L2-normalize at ingestion and your downstream similarity uses cosine, that's fine. Redwood's reranker and similarity primitives support both normalized vectors and raw vectors — we recommend keeping L2-normalized vectors if you're doing cosine locally.

3) Batching & upserts:
- For nightly bulk: use our bulk upsert endpoint (multipart upload + manifest) to ingest efficiently.
- For realtime: prefer batching to ~32-128 vectors per request; our SDK performs automatic batching if you pass an array, and you can tune batch window.

4) SDK/auth:
- SDK supports API key (quickstart), OAuth for fine-grained scoping, and mTLS for Private installs. For KMS integration we support envelope encryption with customer-managed keys.

5) Routing & multi-environment:
- We can route read traffic to a lower-cost replica region and keep writes in the primary for consistency. We'll show a sample routing policy in the deep-dive.

6) Reranker integration:
- Two common patterns: (a) embeddings -> candidate generation (cosine) -> model rerank; (b) embeddings as dense features to the supervised reranker. Both are supported; we'll benchmark latency implications for your topologies.

I'll prepare a short demo of SDK usage (auth, bulk upsert, streaming upserts, and a sample normalization helper). Any specific constraints on vector store (you mentioned you run FAISS on-prem)? We can show compatibility notes.

—Dev
